transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, uh… so what brought me in is mostly that people keep telling me I’m not listening. Like my supervisor at work will be talking right to me, or my wife will be saying something at home, and I’ll be looking at them, but then a minute later I realize I only got like half of what they said.

And then I’m asking them to repeat it, which… you know, that doesn’t go over great. My supervisor especially, he gets this look like I’m doing it on purpose. I’m not, though. It’s just like my mind kind of slips off, even when I’m trying to pay attention.
Do you find yourself having similar problems with staying focused in other situations, like when you're out with friends or doing something you enjoy?

Yeah, I mean… it’s sort of the same thing, I guess. People will be talking right to me, like my supervisor or my wife, and I’m looking at them, I’m not trying to be rude, but then a minute later I realize I only caught maybe half of it.

Then I have to ask them to say it again, and that’s when it turns into a whole thing. Like at work especially, my supervisor gets annoyed, and then I start thinking about that look he gives me, and then—sorry, I know you asked about other situations. It’s just mostly that people keep saying I’m not listening, when I really thought I was.
Do you also find it hard to stay focused when you're not directly involved in a conversation, like when you're reading, watching TV, or working on a task by yourself?

I’m not sure, honestly. Like, reading… I don’t really sit down and read much besides maybe something for work or stuff on my phone, so I don’t know if I’d notice it the same way.

TV, I mean, sometimes it’s just on, you know? My wife likes certain shows and I’ll be in the room, but I’m not always the one picking it, so I don’t know if that counts as me trying to focus on it. Tasks by myself… I guess I’d have to think about that. I notice it more when somebody’s talking to me and then they get annoyed because I missed something. That’s the part that stands out.
When you're working on tasks that require focus, like planning something, organizing your work, or even just finishing a project, do you find it hard to stay on track or get easily distracted?

I mean… maybe? I’m not totally sure how to separate that out. At work, a lot of stuff is kind of routine, so I just do the next thing in front of me. If it’s something where I have to plan it out, I guess I don’t really think of it like “organizing,” I just sort of… start doing it.

But then, like, if someone comes by and says something, or there’s a machine acting up, I’ll get pulled into that, and then later I’m like, wait, what was I doing? Sorry, I don’t know if that’s what you mean. I notice the listening thing more than anything, because people actually call me out on that.
Looking back, when you were in school or growing up, did you have similar issues with focusing or staying attentive, or is this something that started more recently as an adult?

No, this was definitely there when I was a kid. I mean, I wasn’t thinking about it like “focus” back then, but teachers were always moving my seat around because I couldn’t stay put or I’d be messing with something.

I remember getting in trouble for blurting out answers before they finished asking, and I’d kind of lean into other kids’ work or jump in when they were doing something. This was before middle school, even. My mom used to get those calls and then I’d be grounded, and—sorry, I’m getting off track. But yeah, it’s not just something that started as an adult.
Do you find yourself feeling restless, having trouble staying seated, or acting on impulse without thinking things through?

Yeah… restless, definitely. Like if I have to sit still, it’s not just “I’m bored,” it’s like this pressure builds up in my chest and my legs, and I feel like I need to move or do something right then. Like I’m gonna crawl out of my skin if I don’t.

It’s hard to explain without sounding dramatic, but that’s what it feels like. Even sitting here, I’m kind of aware of it—like, okay, don’t keep shifting around too much. And then I start thinking about whether I’m doing it, which makes it worse, kind of.
Have you ever found yourself doing things without really thinking about the consequences, like interrupting others, making quick decisions you later regret, or feeling like you can’t wait your turn?

Yeah… I mean, I do that at work more than I probably want to admit. Like if I see a coworker setting something up and I think they’re doing it wrong, I’ll just step in—sometimes literally reach in and start adjusting it or telling them, “No, do it this way,” before they even ask.

And then it turns into a thing, because I didn’t wait or let them finish. I’m not trying to be a jerk, I just see it and react, like my hands are already moving before I’ve really thought about whether it’s my place. Then later I’m like, yeah, I probably should’ve kept out of it. It’s caused arguments, definitely.
Do you find yourself getting up often when you need to stay seated, or acting impulsively in situations outside of work—like at home, in social settings, or when you're out running errands?

Yeah, I do. The clearest one is at work, when I’m supposed to stay right at my station. I’ll step away to check something, or grab a tool, or go ask somebody something, and I know the line needs me there.

And it’s not always like I made a plan to leave, it’s more like—oh, that thing needs checking, or I should tell him this real quick—and then I’m already walking. Then I come back and realize, yeah, I probably shouldn’t have left right then.

Looking back, did you experience the same restlessness or impulsivity as a child, like getting up often when you were supposed to stay seated or acting without thinking, and did these behaviors continue as you got older?

Yeah, yeah, I was like this as a kid too. Teachers were always moving my seat around because I couldn’t stay put or I’d be messing with something, leaning over, talking—just not staying where I was supposed to.

And I remember calling out answers a lot. Like I’d know it and just say it before they finished asking, which… at the time I thought I was helping, I guess. Or I’d butt into other kids’ work, like if someone was doing a worksheet or building something, I’d jump in and be like, “No, do it like this,” and then I’d get in trouble for not minding my own business.

That was before middle school, definitely. And it didn’t really go away, it just kind of changed as I got older. Like now it’s work stuff instead of classroom stuff.
